title: Preparing newly caught leeches before use
summary: Leeches kept by hunters are tamed and bite readily; newly caught ones are kept one day and fed a little blood so their venomous quality is squeezed out.
quote: Those newly caught must be kept for one day, with a little blood thrown in to them for nourishment; for in this way their venomous quality will be squeezed out.
note: ἐκμειλίττουσαι ('tamed') describes leeches kept in captivity. Authenticity of this short tract is doubted; it is often assigned to Antyllus or a later compiler (outside knowledge).

title: Preparing the skin for leech application
summary: The part to be leeched is first rubbed with natron and smeared, or scratched with the nails, so the leeches take hold more readily.
quote: let the part that is to be leeched be first rubbed with natron and smeared over, or scratched with the nails, for so they will take hold more readily.
note: Greek προεκνιτρούσθω = 'be rubbed beforehand with natron (nitron)'.

title: Applying leeches; snipping tails; salt or ash to detach
summary: Leeches are placed in lukewarm water, handled with a sponge, and warm oil poured over the part; if they draw little, their tails are snipped so they keep drawing until salt or ash is sprinkled on their mouths.
quote: If they should take hold only a little, one must snip off their tails; for as the blood pours out, they do not cease drawing until we sprinkle salt or ash upon their mouths.
note: Hands or feet are immersed in the water holding the leeches. After they fall off, a cupping-glass draws out the 'venomous' matter.

title: Dressings for leech bites and bleeding after leeching
summary: Slight oozing is treated with cumin or flour and wool with a little oil; haemorrhage with vinegar-soaked linen, burnt oak-gall, or a sponge dipped in liquid pitch and burnt.
quote: linen cloths soaked in vinegar are to be applied, or burnt oak-gall, or one must soak a sponge in liquid pitch, burn it, and apply it.
note: Liquid pitch = ὑγροπίσσῃ.

title: Leeches draw only superficial blood
summary: Leeches do not draw the blood that lies deep but suck the blood next to the flesh; they are used in place of cupping-glasses and removed when half the intended blood is drawn, since they are cold by nature.
quote: leeches do not draw the blood that lies in the depth, but suck in that which lies next to the flesh.

title: Revulsion: cupping at the hypochondrium for nosebleed and uterine flow
summary: Revulsion diverts humours away from a part: towards the hands for thorax and belly, vomiting for downward flows, sharp clysters against vomiting; cupping beside the breasts or pressed on the hypochondrium checks nosebleed and excessive menstrual flow.
quote: with those pressed firmly upon the hypochondrium you will revulse the rush of blood towards the nostrils, just as also the immoderate flow through the womb.
note: Breasts = τιτθούς (παρὰ τοὺς τιτθοὺς προβαλλομένη σικύα).

title: Acrid drugs applied to the 'kolpoi'
summary: The draft leaves κόλποις untranslated ('kolpoi'): acrid drugs applied there draw humours back from head and viscera.
quote: Acrid drugs, too, applied to the kolpoi
note: κόλποι is ambiguous (hollows, folds, sinuses, possibly the vagina/womb in gynaecological usage); the referent here is unclear and needs a specialist reading.

title: List of the powers of the cupping-glass
summary: The cupping-glass evacuates matter, resolves pain, reduces inflammation, disperses wind, restores appetite, tones a slack stomach, relieves fainting, transfers deep fluxes, checks haemorrhage and promotes menses.
quote: The cupping-glass is able to evacuate the matter, to resolve pain, to diminish inflammation, to disperse flatulence, to restore the appetites, to make a slack stomach toned, to deliver from faintings
note: At the very beginning of an affection repellents (ἀποκρουστικοῖς) are used instead.

title: Scarifying the legs after suppressed haemorrhoids
summary: When haemorrhoidal bleeding has been suppressed, the legs are scarified after bathing or fomentation; scarification also helps chronic eye fluxes, head conditions, chest and upper back affections, quinsies.
quote: when haemorrhoids have been suppressed, we scarify the legs, having first bathed the patient, or fomenting (πυριᾷν) either in hot water or
note: 'Impactions' at the end renders σφηνώσεις (wedgings, obstructions).

title: Against frequent venesection: loss of vital pneuma
summary: The author will not open a vein many times a year, because vital pneuma is evacuated with the blood, chilling the body and worsening psychic functions; removal should be from less important parts like the legs.
quote: For I have not considered it suitable to open a vein many times in the year; for together with a great quantity of blood the vital pneuma is evacuated along with it
note: First-person statement; if the tract is not Galen's, this is the compiler's view.

title: Why healthy bodies purge badly
summary: Healthy people purge with dizziness, griping and exhaustion because the drug, lacking its proper humour, melts blood and flesh to draw it.
quote: the cathartic drug strives to draw the humour proper to it, and, being at a loss for it, melts down the blood and the flesh
note: Attractive (selective) theory of purgatives, argued at length in De purgantium medicamentorum facultate.

title: Preventive spring evacuation against gout, apoplexy, epilepsy
summary: People liable to illness are evacuated at the onset of spring, by phlebotomy for plethoric diseases or purgation for corruption; Galen claims years of prevention of podagra and early arthritis before tophi formed, and of apoplexy, epilepsy and melancholy.
quote: We, at any rate, have by means of such evacuation prevented, for many years indeed, both podagra and arthritis that was beginning and had not yet produced tophi about the joints from coming about.
note: Tophi = πώρους.

title: Yearly melancholic purged in spring and autumn
summary: A man who falls into melancholy every year unless purged is purged by Galen in both spring and autumn.
quote: a certain man is seized by melancholy every year if he is not purged, and I purge him not only in spring but also in autumn.

title: Woman with breast cancer treated by black-bile purgation
summary: Galen cured a woman's cancerous condition of the breast by strong evacuation with a black-bile purgative and purges her every spring; if omitted, deep pain returns.
quote: I likewise evacuate a certain woman every year at the onset of spring, who had a cancerous condition in the breast, which I cured by evacuating her strongly with a drug that purges black bile.
note: Continuation (pain returns if purgation is omitted) in K11.344-345.

title: Incipient elephas controlled by yearly purgation
summary: A man with beginning elephas (elephantiasis) was cured by phlebotomy and purgation; one purgation a year now suffices, and omitting it brings back signs of the disease.
quote: In another man I cured an incipient elephas at first by phlebotomy and purgation, and each year thereafter a single purgation suffices for him too

title: Summer tertians prevented by late-spring bile purge
summary: A man always seized by tertian fevers in summer has had no fever for many years since Galen purged him of yellow bile in advance at the end of spring.
quote: Another man, who was always seized by tertian fevers in the season of summer, has now for many years not had a fever, being purged of yellow bile by us in anticipation at the end of spring.

title: Which humour to purge for which chronic disease
summary: Elephas and similar need purging of black humours; epileptic, apoplectic and asthmatic diseases of phlegm; hot arthritic diseases of yellow bile, cold-swelling ones of phlegm.
quote: epileptic, apoplectic and asthmatic diseases, of the phlegmatic humours; arthritic diseases, those accompanied by much heat, of the bitter-bilious humours

title: Preparing a patient for hellebore
summary: Before hellebore, thick humours are thinned and passages opened; the patient's response to vomiting is tested with moderate emetics, he is habituated to vomit, and the body is moistened with abundant bland food and rest.
quote: In those who are about to take hellebore, one must first make trial of their nature, to see how it stands with regard to upward purgations, that is, those through vomiting.
note: Neglect brings griping, vertigo, nausea, bad pulse and faintness.

title: Radishes with oxymel spiked with white hellebore
summary: A weak hellebore purge: radishes with oxymel into which sprigs of white hellebore have been fixed for a whole day and night.
quote: We have sometimes given radishes with oxymel, having fixed into them for a whole day and night sprigs of white hellebore; and such a purgation from hellebore would be a weak one.
note: A known mild hellebore preparation (cf. Hippocratic and later ῥαφανὶς ἐλλεβορισμένη; outside knowledge).

title: Narrow-chested patients and emetics: vessel rupture
summary: People with a narrow, compressed thorax are most unsuited to emetic purges, especially white hellebore, because a vessel in the respiratory organs ruptures.
quote: Those who have a narrow (στέρνον ἔχοντε) thorax, and for this reason also a compressed one, happen to be most unsuited to purgations by means of emetic drugs
note: Same unit: bile is evacuated upward, phlegm downward (sometimes reversed), melancholic humour always downward.

title: 'Narrow' thorax rests on a corrupt στέρνον ἔχοντε
summary: The draft renders 'narrow' though the Greek reads στέρνον ἔχοντε ('having a chest'), which makes no sense as it stands.
quote: Those who have a narrow (στέρνον ἔχοντε) thorax
note: Probably a corruption of στενὸν ἔχοντες ('having narrow'); the dual ἔχοντε is also odd. The draft's sense is likely right, but it is an emendation.

title: Hippocratic Aphorism on seasonal direction of purging
summary: Citing the Aphorisms: in summer purge the upper cavity, in winter the lower; analogous reasoning applies to regions, ages and habit (those used to vomiting tolerate upward purges).
quote: It is written in the Aphorisms of Hippocrates concerning the seasons: in summer purge
note: Hippocrates, Aphorisms IV.4 (outside knowledge).

title: Purging regimens for three kinds of dropsy and jaundice
summary: Phlegmatic dropsy: phlegm-drawing drug via lower belly, then vomits, then apophlegmatisms; ascites: a hydragogue; jaundice: a cholagogue, with bile expelled up, down, by urine, palate and nostrils.
quote: in the case of the ascitic dropsy we shall give one of the hydragogue drugs, just as in the case of the icteric one of the cholagogue drugs.
note: Apophlegmatisms = ἀποφλεγματισμῶν (errhines/masticatories drawing phlegm from the head).

title: Purge upward in paroxysms, downward in remissions
summary: Evacuations should be made from the upper parts during paroxysms and from the lower parts during remissions, imitating spontaneous vomiting and nosebleeds in paroxysms and urine and stools in remissions.
quote: making the evacuations from the upper parts during the paroxysms, and from the [350] lower parts during the so-called remissions.

title: Unmixed melikraton boiled with thinning herbs
summary: When an acute disease must be purged early, preparation may use unmixed melikraton boiled with hyssop, thyme, origanum, goat's-origanum or pennyroyal to thin the humours.
quote: unmixed melikraton made and given, having boiled in it some hyssop, or thyme, or origanum, or goat's-origanum, or pennyroyal

title: Definition of humours 'in turgor' (orgân)
summary: Humours are said to be in turgor when, in violent motion and flowing between parts at the start of a disease, they cause pain, nausea and restlessness; only these may be purged early.
quote: The humours are said to be in turgor when, having come into a more violent motion and flowing across from parts to parts, at the beginning of the disease they trouble the person
note: Gloss on Hippocratic ὀργᾶν (Aph. I.22).

title: Best hiera: with hellebore, without scammony
summary: Of the variously prepared hiera, the version containing hellebore but not scammony is the best laxative.
quote: the version that has taken hellebore but does not contain scammony is the best laxative drug.

title: Sipping ptisane after a cathartic (Hippocrates)
summary: After the cathartic is drunk the patient sips ptisane juice to wash residue from gullet and stomach and temper the drug; once purging begins ptisane is stopped so as not to dissipate it.
quote: After the cathartic has been taken it is beneficial to sip ptisane afterwards, as Hippocrates says.

title: Why a purgative sometimes fails
summary: A purge may fail from the patient's nature, too small a dose, hard faeces lodged in the intestine (removable by a prior clyster), or nature turning to urine; failed drugs may even nourish, or act as poisons.
quote: hard faeces wedged in one of the intestines, which could have been evacuated by means of a clyster before the purging drug was given, prevents the evacuation.
note: Checks flagged this unit 'fail'; 'hard faeces ... prevents' shows a grammatical slip in the draft.

title: Fragrant seeds mixed into purgatives to protect the stomach
summary: Since purgatives harm the belly and its sinewy, sensitive mouth, fragrant seeds of attenuating and incisive power are mixed in to blunt harm without hindering action.
quote: the admixture of fragrant substances was devised, so that their power might not touch the body of the belly alone and unmixed.

title: Asclepiades: 'openly shameless' opponent of attraction
summary: Asclepiades is named as one who, unlike anyone in Hippocrates' time, shamelessly fought the truth that purgatives attract their proper humour.
quote: Asclepiades, who was openly shameless and stripped, as it were, for some prize (ἔπαθλόν τινα) against the truth
note: Asclepiades of Bithynia (fl. c. 100 BC), corpuscular theorist who denied natural faculties (outside knowledge).

title: Erasistratus never recognises the attractive power
summary: Erasistratus, more modest, still overturns the main point: nowhere in his writings does he know the attractive power, substituting 'following toward what is being emptied'.
quote: the attractive power, Erasistratus knows nowhere in his own writings, but rather employs in its place the following toward what is being emptied.
note: Refers to Erasistratus' principle of horror vacui (πρὸς τὸ κενούμενον ἀκολουθία; outside knowledge).

title: Opponents' theory: purgatives transform humours into their own kind
summary: The opponents hold that a purgative changes any humour it touches into its own form: cholagogues make yellow bile, phlegmagogues phlegm, hydragogues water, another black bile.
quote: The purgative drug alters whatever humour it touches into its own form: the one they name cholagogue producing yellow bile, just as the one they call phlegmagogue produces phlegm

title: Asclepiadean and Erasistratean views of phlebotomy vs purgation
summary: For the Asclepiadeans phlebotomy removes all humours equally while purgation removes the others to leave the blood pure; for the Erasistrateans both evacuate equally, purgation adding corruption of what is evacuated.
quote: According to Erasistratus and his followers, the evacuation of all the humours is equal, as in phlebotomies, so also in purgations
note: Greek has τοὺς Ἀσκληπιάδας and in K11.326-327 οἱ Ἀσκληπιάδαι, rendered 'Asclepiadeans'/'Asclepiadae'. Whether this means followers of Asclepiades or the Asclepiad guild is unclear; context suggests followers of Asclepiades.

title: Rome, 'this most populous city', full of jaundiced and dropsical
summary: Galen challenges the sophists to a public contest of deeds in the city where countless jaundiced and dropsical patients can be found every day.
quote: with the very deeds to which I summon them in this most populous city, in which countless jaundiced persons can be found every day, and countless dropsical ones.
note: The city is Rome (named at K11.340-341).

title: Galen's public demonstration: one cholagogue purge cures jaundice
summary: Given a feverless jaundiced man full of bile, Galen prepares him for some days and, at the right moment, restores his natural state with a single bile-drawing laxative and nothing else.
quote: by giving one of the bile-drawing laxatives (ὑπήλατον), I bring the man back to his natural state by means of such a purgation, without undertaking anything further at all with regard to the body.
note: K11.329 adds that he has shown this many times and converted many.

title: Unnamed sophist: drugs draw like sucking things, thinnest first
summary: A sophist, when cornered, claimed each drug simply draws like a sucking creature, the thinner humours following first, then thicker, then thickest.
quote: each of them simply draws, like the things that suck (βδάλλοντα); and that what is thinner among the humours follows the attraction first, next after it the thicker, and then in this way the thickest.
note: Probably an Erasistratean or Asclepiadean contemporary in Rome; unnamed.

title: Galen's overnight refutation book handed to the sophist's pupils
summary: The sophist was applauded and fled; next day Galen gave his 'chorus' a book refuting him, quoted as beginning 'Yesterday you ran away from the argument'.
quote: when on the following day a certain book was given by us to his chorus-members, in which there was a refutation of what had thus suddenly been ventured
note: An otherwise unattested polemical pamphlet; the quoted text continues into K11.332-333.

title: Black bile as the lees of blood, like lees in wine
summary: Black bile is described as a sort of sediment of the blood, as lees are in wine.
quote: although it is, as it were, a kind of sediment of the blood, as the lees are in wines.
note: Greek ἰλύς (sediment) and τρύξ (wine lees).

title: Blood-drawing drugs exist but are poisons Galen will not name
summary: Some drugs draw blood from the start through stomach and intestine vessels; physicians class them as deleterious poisons, and Galen refuses to write their names.
quote: As for the names of such drugs, even if I knew them with certainty, I would not disclose them in writing.

title: Poisonings among the Thracian Bithynians in Galen's childhood
summary: When Galen was a child, among the Thracian Bithynians a man found a herb that made those who took it pass blood and die.
quote: what happened among the Thracian Bithynians when we were still children. A certain man found a herb of such a kind that whoever took some of it excreted blood and so perished.
note: Galen was born 129 CE at Pergamum; 'Thracian Bithynians' (Herodotus' Thracian origin of the Bithynians) places this in Bithynia, neighbouring Mysia (outside knowledge).

title: Poisoner discovers blood-drawing herb via a pig's liver; executed blindfold
summary: Under torture the poisoner said he saw bloody ichor flow from a pig's liver set on a plant, tested it on a passer-by, and used it for murder; the governor had him led to execution blindfolded so he could not point out the abundant plant.
quote: ordered him to be led away to be put to death with his eyes bound, so that he might not show it to anyone on the way.
note: 'Governor of the people' renders ὁ τοῦ ἔθνους ἡγούμενος, i.e. the provincial governor.

title: 'When his belly had become fixed' in the poisoner story
summary: The draft renders πηξάσης τῆς γαστρός literally as the belly 'becoming fixed', the reason the man set the liver down.
quote: when his belly had become fixed (πηξάσης τῆς γαστρός), he set it down upon a plant
note: The sense is unclear: possibly a sudden call of nature, a cramp, or a textual problem. Literal rendering leaves the narrative opaque.

title: Poison recipes should be kept silent
summary: Galen condemns writers who 'with monstrous liberality' set down preparations of poisons, saying sensible men keep them silent.
quote: there have already been some who were ungrudging even in the teaching of these things, displaying a kind of monstrous liberality and writing down the preparations of each of the poisons

title: Laymen mock disputing physicians as 'logiatroi'
summary: Hearing physicians contradict each other, the public laughs, condemns reasoning, and calls such men 'word-physicians'.
quote: they call those who utter anything at all "word-physicians" (logiatroi).
note: Rare term λογίατρος; Galen adds that every layman is better than such a sophist.

title: Layman with ulcerous eruptions refuses phlebotomy
summary: A sensible layman with sudden ulcerous, discoloured eruptions demanded purging; told to be bled, he answered that the good would be evacuated with the corrupted.
quote: 'Are you not mad?' he said, 'for it stands to reason that the good will be evacuated together with the corrupted.'

title: Galen's cures by purgation alone and the hatred they earned
summary: Rivals hated Galen for curing by purgation alone alopecia, incipient cancer, elephas, phagedaena, scotoma, mania, epilepsy, melancholy, headache and sciatica.
quote: another because I completely cured maniacal, epileptic and melancholic patients, and moreover not a few suffering from cephalaea, by purgations alone, just as I did sciatic patients too.

title: Supposed colic patient cured by purgation after three months
summary: A man treated three months as a colic case and worsening was cured by Galen with purgation alone after discarding the other remedies.
quote: that man recently who had already been treated for three months by the physicians as a colic patient and was progressing toward the worse

title: Female flux in a prominent Roman woman cured by purgation
summary: Galen cured a uterine flux in a not inconspicuous woman at Rome, and in many obscurer women, by purgation alone.
quote: I also cured a female flux, in a certain not inconspicuous one of the women at Rome, by purgations alone

title: Erysipelas: cholagogue best, phlegmagogue worst
summary: For erysipelas no remedy is more effective than a bile-drawing drug, and the phlegm-drawing drug is most contrary.
quote: as for erysipelata, what need is there even to say that there is no more effective remedy than a bile-drawing drug

title: Hippocratic maxims on beginnings and acme
summary: Quoting Hippocrates: at the beginning of diseases move what needs moving, at the acme keep quiet; and around beginnings and ends all things are weaker.
quote: "When diseases are beginning, if anything seems to need moving, move it; but when they are at their acme, it is better to keep quiet."
note: Hippocrates, Aphorisms II.29 and II.30; purging maxims from Aph. I.22-24 follow (outside knowledge).

title: On Crises, book 1: recognising the beginning
summary: Galen refers to the first book of On Crises, where he showed how to recognise the first period, chiefly by lack of concoction.
quote: Many things, then, have been said by me about this beginning also in the first book of On Crises
note: Also argues the beginning cannot be the same for diseases resolved by day 7 and a quartan lasting a year.

title: On Uneven Dyscrasia and On Tumours contrary to Nature
summary: Galen cites these treatises for the theory of inflammation, listing rival mechanisms: paremptosis, wedging-in of vessels, blocking of masses in pores.
quote: as we taught both in the treatise On Uneven Dyskrasia and in that On Tumours contrary to Nature
note: Paremptosis and sphenosis are Erasistratean concepts (outside knowledge).

title: Periods of an inflammation: filling, putrefaction, pus, decline
summary: An inflammation begins while the part fills with blood; it increases as contents putrefy, generating heat and pneuma; the acme is while pus forms, with greatest pain; decline follows suppuration or dispersal.
quote: For the pains and the fevers occur around the generation of the pus rather than once it has been generated

title: Concoction signs in ophthalmia and nasal catarrh
summary: In ophthalmia discharge goes from copious and thin to scanty and thick, gluing the eyelids by rheum; nasal flux that thickens and brings mucus (myxa) and phlegm (blenna) signals concoction.
quote: the eyelids of those who have slept are even glued together by the rheum (lēmē) that has formed

title: Hippocrates on shoulder dislocation: 'I do not insist'
summary: Galen imitates Hippocrates' reserve on the shoulder dislocation and declines the logical question whether the acme has duration.
quote: "I, for my part, do not insist upon this, although I have something I could say."
note: Hippocrates, On Joints 1 (outside knowledge).

title: Archigenes mixes logical inquiries into medical treatises
summary: Archigenes is criticised as one who brings everything into everything, mixing inquiries about names and logical matters into strictly medical treatises.
quote: as those do who bring everything into everything, one of whom is Archigenes. For this man mixes into the most strictly medical treatises sometimes an inquiry about names
note: Archigenes of Apamea, Pneumatist, active under Trajan (outside knowledge).

title: Prime of hunting dogs, racehorses and athletes
summary: Hunting dogs and racehorses stay at peak strength two or three years; human athletes often four or five, illustrating an acme with breadth.
quote: human athletes who have remained equal in strength, so far as perception goes, not for these three years only, but often for four and five.

title: No disease attacks at its acme; synochos needs 3-4 hours
summary: Even the synochos fever takes at least three or four hours to reach full acme, and apoplexy and epilepsy pass quickly through beginning and increase; even a beheading has successive moments.
quote: from the first onset to the most complete acme it arrives in four or three hours at the very least

title: Scirrhous leg swellings growing over three or four years
summary: Galen has often seen scirrhous swellings of the legs form without prior inflammation and grow slowly over three or four years before hindering walking.
quote: I have often observed scirrhous swellings in the legs forming right from the beginning without an inflammation having preceded them, and increasing little by little over three and sometimes even four years

title: Hidden scirrhus of the liver revealed by dropsy and wasting
summary: A scirrhous tumour in the concave liver may escape notice until dropsy follows; Galen saw many where a large tumour suddenly appeared once it reached the convex parts and the hypochondrial muscles wasted.
quote: At any rate I have seen not a few who, along such a course of symptoms, in a short time brought to light a not small tumour in a scirrhous liver

title: Good and deadly urines
summary: Best urine is well-coloured, moderately thick, with good suspended matter, cloud or sediment; water-like urine is unconcocted; black cloud or sediment, dusky, bran-like, foul-smelling or oily urine is deadly.
quote: urine that is strongly foul-smelling, and that which is fatty, which they call oily, is deadly.

title: On the Differentiae of Diseases
summary: Galen says the genera, differentiae and species of diseases are set out in a single treatise titled On the Differentiae of Diseases.
quote: have been set out in a single treatise, which is entitled On the Differentiae of Diseases.

title: Feeding by disease period; remission defined
summary: Treatment is soothing at the acme and combative at beginning and end; if strength will last, food is withheld until decline, otherwise the patient is fed from the start in remissions.
quote: if it will hold out until the time of the acme even without taking nourishment, it is best to abstain from food until the decline has begun
note: Refers to 'the treatise on the therapeutic method' (Methodus medendi).

title: Archigenes' two books on the periods in diseases
summary: Galen says Archigenes turned aside into prolixity, in all his writings and in the two books he wrote on periods in diseases, burdening readers with useless matters.
quote: as did Archigenes both in all his other writings and in the two books which he wrote on the periods in diseases.
note: A lost work of Archigenes; also K7.461-462.

title: Homer uses 'coma' for sleep
summary: Galen cites two Homeric lines where coma seems to mean sleep, contrasting Hippocratic usage.
quote: "Truly a soft coma enfolded me, suffering terribly as I was."
note: Odyssey 18.201 and Iliad 14.359 (outside knowledge).

title: Prorrhetic: sleepless comatose patients, 'are they phrenitic?'
summary: Hippocrates' Prorrhetic asks whether those comatose at the start, with pain of head, loins, hypochondrium and neck and sleepless, are phrenitic.
quote: "Those who become comatose at the beginnings, with pain of the head, loins, hypochondrium, neck, being sleepless — are they phrenitic?"
note: Prorrhetic I.1 (outside knowledge).

title: Commentators derive 'comatose' from kōmazein (revelling)
summary: Some commentators said the comatose are named from revellers, who stay awake, have moist red unsteady eyes and uncontrolled movements.
quote: some of the commentators say that the comatose are named from revelling (kōmazein); for those who revel are awake, and the comatose are awake as well.

title: Galen's rule for the good exegete
summary: A good interpreter must show not only that an explanation is plausible or true but that it fits the author's own opinion, drawn from the author himself.
quote: I do not think that the good exegete should consider this alone, whether he has spoken plausibly or truly, but also whether it adheres to the opinion of the author

title: Slave's wife after miscarriage at five months
summary: Epidemics III: a household slave's wife, after miscarriage at about five months, had fever; at first comatose, then sleepless.
quote: "Another woman, after a miscarriage at about the fifth month, the wife of a household slave, fever seized; at the beginning she was comatose, and then again

title: Thasos: the Parian lodging above the Artemision
summary: Epidemics III case of the Parian at Thasos who lay sick above the Artemision, seized by acute, continuous, burning fever.
quote: "In Thasos the Parian, who lay sick above the Artemision, an acute fever seized
note: Temple of Artemis on Thasos (outside knowledge).

title: Thasos woman lodging by the 'Market of Liars'
summary: Epidemics III woman lying sick at the Market of Liars after a difficult first birth of a son, with rigors, delirium and later coma.
quote: a woman who lay sick in the Market of Liars (ἐπὶ ψευδέων ἀγορῇ), having then for the first time given birth, with difficulty, to a male child
note: A Thasian place name in Epidemics III (outside knowledge).

title: Abbreviated Greek 'ἀπιότ. καὶ ἀχειρόπ.' left in the draft
summary: The draft carries untranslated abbreviated Greek in the description of the Parian's irregular illness.
quote: often made many changes (ἀπιότ. καὶ ἀχειρόπ.) towards the opposite conditions
note: The Kühn text itself is abbreviated here; the words are probably forms of ἀπιστότερον/ἀχειροποίητον or similar, and the rendering is a guess.

title: Parotid swellings that never suppurated
summary: In the constitution described, swellings by the ears came in feverless, ambulant people, on one or both sides, and subsided harmlessly without suppurating or inflammation.
quote: they subsided in all without harm, and did not suppurate in any, as do those arising from other causes.
note: The mumps constitution of Epidemics I (outside knowledge), though Galen says it is from the 'same book'.

title: Pythion: comatose on the ninth day
summary: Epidemics III, Pythion: on the ninth day comatose and nauseated when roused; here coma means a kind of kataphora.
quote: in the case of Pythion, he says, "on the ninth day comatose, nauseated when he was roused"

title: Two kinds of kataphora: somnolent and sleepless
summary: Both kinds cannot raise their eyes and are weighed down; one sleeps deeply and long, the other stays sleepless, tossing as phantasms interrupt sleep.
quote: whereas the others are sleepless, tossing about, as one phantasm supervenes upon another, stirring the mind and interrupting sleep
note: Checks flagged unit 'fail'.

title: 'Typhomania' as a supposed mixture of lethargy and phrenitis
summary: Uneducated physicians and self-styled Hippocrateans called phrenitics who lie still like lethargics 'typhomania', a mixture of lethargy and phrenitis.
quote: while some suppose it to be a mixture compounded of lethargy and phrenitis, and name it typhomania.
note: Typhomania is a term otherwise found in later authors (outside knowledge).

title: Hippocrates never uses epithets idly, unlike Homer
summary: Homer says 'liquid oil' and 'white milk' with no distinction, but with Hippocrates every word and syllable signifies something real.
quote: nor does he say, as Homer does, 'liquid oil' and 'white milk' for the sake of no distinction at all

title: Hippocrates' graded vocabulary for derangement
summary: Galen lists Hippocratic verbs for derangement (παρελήρει, παρηνέχθη, παρέκοψε, παρεφρόνησε, ἐξέστη, ἐμάνη, ἐξεμάνη, οὐ κατενόει, παρέλεγε), each marking a degree.
quote: for each magnitude of the species of derangement he has devised a proper name.

title: 'While being heated, dined': Hippocrates' gradation of fever
summary: Hippocrates would not call 'fever' a heat during which one can dine, and wrote 'fire seized him' for great fever.
quote: For "a man," he says, "while being heated, dined": he did not venture to call "fever" a heat of such a degree during which one is able to dine.

title: Sluggish (nōthra) wakeful kataphora distinguished from lethargy
summary: Wakeful kataphora has two species, one called sluggish; such patients rave and want to get up, react to voices and touch, and move spasmodically, unlike motionless, voiceless lethargics.
quote: for they readily get up on hearing a voice or any sound at all, and if you touch some part of the body, they at once raise their eyes and look toward the one touching them.

title: Odd rendering 'incoherently (χωρίς) and in a knavish manner'
summary: The draft renders χωρὶς and πανούργως in a description of lethargics in a way that reads oddly.
quote: For neither do they say anything incoherently (χωρίς) and in a knavish manner (πανούργως)
note: The Greek appears corrupt (χωρὶς φράζουσι ... πανούργως); 'knavish' for πανούργως is doubtful here.

title: Two readings of the Prorrhetic: with or without 'are they'
summary: The Prorrhetic sentence circulated in copies with and without εἰσίν ('are they'), i.e. 'are they then phrenitic?' versus 'then phrenitic?'.
quote: This saying is written in two ways: in some copies thus, but in some without the "are they", "are they then phrenitic?"
note: Evidence of textual variants in Galen's copies; returned to at K7.664-665.

title: Commentators read ἆρα as syllogistic, not aporetic
summary: Some interpreters said Hippocrates' ἆρα is syllogistic ('therefore'); Galen argues from word order and Greek usage that the preposed ἆρά γε is interrogative.
quote: The word ἆρα, he says, is syllogistic, not aporetic.
note: Galen's grammatical argument continues K7.660-662.

title: Hippocratic parallels for interrogative ἆρα
summary: Galen cites Epidemics I (dysentery after watery urine), Epidemics VI (sediment after urination in children, because warmer?) and Prorrhetic (white evacuation in phrenitics, as in Archecrates).
quote: 'In phrenitics a white evacuation is bad, as also in Archecrates. Does torpor, then, also occur in these cases?'
note: Archecrates is a patient named in Prorrhetic I.

title: Drunkenness as model for sleepless coma
summary: Drunk people are heavy-headed, cannot lift their eyelids yet cannot sleep; similarly an unconcocted fullness of the head at disease onset makes patients comatose and sleepless, ending in recovery, phrenitis or lethargy.
quote: So too, then, when an unconcocted plenitude has taken hold of the head, they are at the same time both sleepless and comatose.

title: Olympic and Pythian periods as model of 'period'
summary: The ancients used 'period' for any same event recurring at equal intervals, as in the Olympic and Pythian periods.
quote: they used to call certain periods Olympic [476] and Pythian.

title: Type-theorists' absurd reckoning: 'twelve twelfth-day fevers'
summary: Faced with a paroxysm anticipating two hours daily, these physicians count a 22-hour period on fingers or a diagram and call it twelve twelfth-day fevers, drawing laughter.
quote: some on their fingers, others even on a diagram drawn in some book, they say that such a type is twelve twelfth-day fevers.

title: Dating: Galen first hears type-theory c. 161 CE
summary: Galen first heard this theory just after Antoninus (Pius), emperor after Hadrian, had died, when the new emperor took the name Antoninus and made Lucius co-ruler.
quote: Antoninus, who became emperor after Hadrian, had recently departed from among men, and at that time Severus was ruling, having renamed himself Antoninus
note: Antoninus Pius died March 161 CE; the accession of Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus dates the episode (outside knowledge).

title: 'Severus' for Verus in the imperial dating
summary: The Greek reads Σεβῆρος (Severus) twice, and the draft follows it, but the emperors meant are Marcus Aurelius (formerly M. Annius Verus) and Lucius Verus.
quote: having taken Lucius into partnership in the rule and renamed him Severus.
note: Probably a confusion or corruption of Οὐῆρος; the draft renders the Greek faithfully but a note is needed.

title: Galen's debate over a 7-hour period (5 h paroxysm, 2 h remission)
summary: Asked what type a 5-hour paroxysm with 2-hour remission makes, Galen replied it cannot occur, since short paroxysms have long declines; the propounder said it was for exercise.
quote: I answered him at once that this cannot even occur. For paroxysms of so short a duration make their declines long, and for the most part even arrive at apyrexia.

title: Only quotidian, tertian and quartan periods exist
summary: All fever paroxysms recur daily, every third day or every fourth day; Galen mocks sophists who claim fifth-, sixth-, seventh-day or longer periods.
quote: all the paroxysms in fevers occur either every day, or every third day, or every fourth day

title: Diagnosis by 'antapodoseis' (correspondences of paroxysms)
summary: Some recognise the three types not by their nature but by correspondences of paroxysms, and so remain ignorant until day four or five.
quote: but from the correspondences (antapodoseis) in the paroxysms—for this is what they themselves are accustomed to call the analogies of the paroxysms.

title: Suspect 'quartan' at the eleventh hour
summary: In an example of coinciding paroxysms, the Greek names a second quartan at the eleventh hour where the logic seems to need a tertian.
quote: the text's τεταρταῖον here is suspect, perhaps for τριταῖον
note: The draft itself flags the problem.

title: Physicians mistake two tertians for one quotidian
summary: Galen often saw attending physicians take an interwoven double tertian for a single quotidian, convincing them only when the earlier tertian resolved and the severer remained.
quote: often in the case of the sick we have seen the attending physicians supposing a complication of two tertians to be a single quotidian

title: Agathinus slipped into type-theory teaching
summary: Even Agathinus, 'a man of no ordinary stature', fell into this sort of teaching, which is still tolerable compared with seven-hour periods.
quote: for even Agathinus, a man of no ordinary stature, slipped into such a form of teaching
note: Agathinus of Sparta, Pneumatist, teacher of Archigenes (outside knowledge).

title: Philistion invoked to mock seven-hour period theorists
summary: Those who posit seven-hour periods need not Galen but Philistion, or someone like him, to make sport of their drivel.
quote: those who make periods of seven hours had need not of us but of Philistion, or of someone of that sort to make sport of their drivel.
note: Almost certainly Philistion the mime-writer (Augustan era), not the physician of Locri (outside knowledge).

title: Types theory as dinner riddles; real fevers to learn
summary: Type-books were exercises for the young like riddles at dinner; better to teach recognition of quotidian, tertian, quartan, semitertian and tertian-natured fevers by their own signs.
quote: they wrote these things as exercises for the young, resembling riddles posed at dinner.

title: Galen wrote this work in one day at younger men's request
summary: Younger men pressed Galen to write down the method he had taught them in jest, and he devoted a single day to it, unwillingly.
quote: for their sake I have devoted a single day, not willingly, to this discourse as well.

title: A whole book on finding kind and number of types
summary: Galen learned that someone wrote a whole, not small, book teaching how to find the kind and number of types for any period; he says the method fits in a few words.
quote: I learned that a certain person has even written a whole book, and not a small one, teaching how one might, for each paroxysmal period proposed, discover both the kind and the number of the types.
note: Author unnamed; lost.

title: Greek numeral νστ΄ for the quintan's 96 hours
summary: The draft gives quintan 96 but notes the Greek numeral νστ΄, which is not a valid numeral for 96 (ϟϛ΄).
quote: for the quintan 96 (νστ΄)
note: Numeral corruption in the transmitted text; 96 is required by the series (24 x 4).

title: Galen's table of type-hours (24 to 1176)
summary: A diagram lists hours per type in steps of 24: quotidian 24, tertian 48, quartan 72 up to the fiftieth-day type at 1176, to be kept on a sheet of papyrus.
quote: either by memory or written down on a sheet of papyrus: for the quotidian that of 24, for the tertian that of forty-eight
note: Table continues in K7.490-491, K7.492 and K7.493; values check arithmetically (nth-day type = (n-1) x 24).

title: 'Five is the twenty-fourth part of 108': numeral error
summary: The draft says a 5-hour period is the 24th part of 108 and yields sextan types, but 5 x 24 = 120, the sextan figure.
quote: But five is the twenty-fourth part of 108
note: The Greek reads ρη΄ (108), evidently a corruption of ρκ΄ (120); the draft renders the corrupt numeral faithfully.

title: Galen trained in arithmetic as a boy
summary: Galen says that thanks to his education, exercised in numbers in boyhood, he answers type problems on the spot, while the untrained need years.
quote: I for my part, in virtue of my education, answer each of these on the spot to those who put them to me, because I was exercised in numbers in my boyhood years

title: Type-theorists disagree on the longest type
summary: Some extend types to fifteen days, some to monthly ones, some to two or three months; Galen notes he has treated Hippocrates on what lies beyond the quartan in other writings.
quote: Some of them suppose that the periods of the types proceed as far as fifteen days; some as far as monthly ones; and there are also those who go as far as two or three months.

title: Books to Hephaestus or cut up for everyday use
summary: Galen says such books should be given to Hephaestus (burned) or will perish with time, nobody copying them, and even being cut up for everyday needs.
quote: let them, being ashamed, at last some day summon Hephaestus upon their books; or, even if they themselves do not summon him, time will destroy them.
note: Evidence for recycling of unwanted papyrus rolls.

title: Nychthemeron and a year of 365 and a quarter days
summary: Here 'day' means day plus night, called by some nychthemeron, just as the year is said to be 365 and a quarter days.
quote: Thus at any rate we also say that the year is of 365 days and a quarter.

title: Inclusive naming of types
summary: Types are named from the return of the paroxysm, not completed days: a period of four days is called a quintan.
quote: when you find a period of a type of four days, you will call it quintan, for it is not the same thing to suffer the paroxysm on every fifth day and to have a period of five days.

title: Treatise already circulated among Galen's companions
summary: Galen notes these things had already been written and given out to some companions before he added the finger method.
quote: These things having already been written and given out to some of my companions
note: Evidence for informal circulation (ἔκδοσις) of Galen's texts.

title: Euclid's Elements cited for greatest common measure
summary: The finger method rests on Euclid's theorem on the greatest common measure of two numbers, cited as in the seventh (book) of the Elements.
quote: And this theorem has been demonstrated also by Euclid in the (book) of the Elements, and it is the seventh chapter of it.
note: Greek τῶν στοιχείων ἕβδομον: 'the seventh of the Elements', i.e. Book VII (VII.2 gives the GCD algorithm); the draft's 'seventh chapter' is a misreading (outside knowledge).

title: Pythian precept: be sparing of time
summary: Galen closes recalling the Pythian precept that one should be sparing of time.
quote: remembering the Pythian precept, that it is fitting to be sparing of time.
note: Delphic maxim (χρόνου φείδου; outside knowledge).

title: Asclepiades and Methodists deny faculty; plethora only relative to vessels
summary: Asclepiades, many Asclepiadeans and Methodists said there is no faculty in animals, so they measure much and little only against vessel space and take indication only from 'constriction'.
quote: the things written [515] by Asclepiades and by many Asclepiadeans and Methodics to the effect that there is no faculty at all in animals
note: 'Constriction' = στέγνωσις, the Methodist common state (outside knowledge).

title: Empiricists' 'plethoric syndrome'
summary: Empiricists claim long experience shows phlebotomy helps a syndrome: distended vessels, redness and heaviness, reluctance to move, tension of limbs, ulcerous and lassitude sensations, idle life with rich diet and suppressed excretions.
quote: Upon this syndrome, at any rate—for so they call the aggregate of symptoms—phlebotomy has been observed to be beneficial.
note: Checks flagged this unit 'fail'.

title: Laymen's words for stomach distress
summary: Laymen describe being weighed down by food, being bitten and gnawed, or, unable to describe it, say they are nauseated (asasthai).
quote: often, being unable to describe accurately what is happening, they say that they are nauseated (ἀσᾶσθαι).

title: PHP, On the Elements, Natural Faculties cited on faculties
summary: Galen refers to On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato (heart, brain, liver as sources of arterial, nervous and venous faculties), On the Elements according to Hippocrates, and On the Natural Faculties.
quote: I also taught that the heart is, as it were, a kind of source of the faculty of the arteries, the brain of that of the nerves, and the liver of that of the veins.
note: 'A certain other treatise' on mixture as substance of faculties: perhaps Quod animi mores (outside knowledge).

title: Stoic cohesive faculty: pneuma holds, matter is held
summary: The Stoics, chief proponents of the cohesive faculty, make pneumatic substance what holds together and material substance what is held: air and fire hold, earth and water are held.
quote: they say that air and fire hold together, while earth and water are held together.

title: Contemporary Herophileans on the cohesive cause
summary: Self-styled Herophileans pronounce on a cohesive faculty binding stones and wood without knowing whether it is air, fire or both, and call their questioners sophists when refuted.
quote: some of those who nowadays call themselves Herophileans, having not even in a dream heard these things, boldly make pronouncements about the cohesive faculty

title: On the Natural Faculties: four faculties
summary: Citing On the Natural Faculties: attractive, alterative, retentive and expulsive faculties; heaviness alone cannot signal plethora relative to each.
quote: one faculty is attractive of what is proper, another alterative of these same things, another a retentive faculty, and a fourth expulsive of what is foreign
note: Unit ends with a garbled clause '(κατὰ τὰ νεῦρα)'; the draft sentence is incomplete.

title: Philippus and Archigenes touched on faculty theory
summary: No one before Galen defined the faculties scientifically; Philippus and Archigenes and their followers touched the theory only slightly; arterial plethora signs are in Galen's pulse treatise.
quote: For Philippus and Archigenes and their followers touched to a small extent upon the theory of them, but none even of these worked it out completely.
note: Philippus is probably the Empiricist/Pneumatist physician also named elsewhere by Galen; identity uncertain (outside knowledge).

title: Liver parenchyma lacks nerves
summary: The flesh of the convex liver, called parenchyma, has no nerve implanted; nerves at the portae are so short they only weave its membrane.
quote: For the nerves implanted in the liver at the portae are so short that they appear to interweave only its membrane.

title: On the Movement of Muscles cited
summary: Whether the limb weighs on the muscle only when moving or also at rest was settled in Galen's writings On the Movement of Muscles.
quote: which has been determined by us in the writings On the Movement of Muscles

title: Erasistratus, Hygiene book 1: genesis of plethora
summary: Erasistratus says when distributed food is not concocted, worked off or excreted, vessels fill and distend until contents push into the adjacent vessels of pneuma.
quote: And when the vessels no longer admit any further packing-in, and other nourishment is brought up from the belly, what is already present takes an impulse towards the adjacent vessels of the pneuma.
note: Galen states (K7.536-537) this is the only work where Erasistratus gives signs of plethos; fragment of a lost work.

title: Erasistratus' signs of plethora quoted
summary: Erasistratus: with moderate filling people seem better-toned and stronger; with more, upper arms, shins and hands fill out; when advanced, they are sore, sluggish, tense, with lassitude, near disease.
quote: when the plethora advances far, these parts are sore, slower and harder to move, and the whole body is tense to the touch, since a lassitude (kopos) appears.

title: Erasistratus' On Fevers: plethora causes paremptosis
summary: For Erasistratus plethora causes paremptosis of blood into arteries, on which inflammations form and fever follows; he ignores faculty-plethora in this book and On Fevers.
quote: For plethora, according to him, is the cause of paremptosis, upon which inflammations are formed and fever follows

title: Trainers' three kinds of fatigue
summary: Precise gymnastic trainers distinguish ulcerous, tensive and inflammatory fatigue; tensive fatigue means limbs 'filled up', inflammation adds throbbing pain.
quote: the more precise of the gymnastic trainers too, when they call one of the fatigues ulcerous, another tensive, and another inflammatory

title: Wine-jars bursting from must turned to pneuma
summary: Not only sinews and ropes burst from tension but often wine-jars, from must that has turned to pneuma.
quote: often also wine-jars, from must that has turned to pneuma.

title: Tin vessel of viper theriac swells and bursts its wrapping
summary: Recently a tin vessel holding the drug made from vipers swelled so much that the leather wrapping and the tying cord burst and the lid bulged.
quote: Recently, at any rate, a tin vessel was so greatly inflated by the drug contained in it, the one prepared from vipers, that both the leather wrapped around it and the cord with which it had been tied burst
note: The viper drug is theriac; fermentation in storage. Unit flagged 'fail' by checks but this passage reads soundly.

title: Four grades of biting: squill to rigor
summary: Biting substances grade into itch-producing (like squill), biting (like onion, ulcerating with time), shivering, and rigor; biting humours act the same four ways.
quote: for those that bite moderately are itch-producing, like squill; those that bite more vehemently are biting, like the onion

title: Cross-references: Causes of Symptoms, Hygiene, Mixtures, Simple Drugs
summary: For biting things Galen refers to book 2 of On the Causes of Symptoms, book 4 of the Hygiene, On the Power of Drugs, and On Mixtures.
quote: what has been said in the second book of On the Causes in the Symptoms and in the fourth of the Hygiene is sufficient
note: 'On the Power of Drugs' is presumably De simplicium medicamentorum facultatibus (outside knowledge).

title: Trainers' treatment of over-exercised athletes
summary: Trainers treat those who exercised too much with abundant oil, soft rubbing and warm baths of sweet water to disperse biting humours formed from melted fat and flesh.
quote: the gymnastic trainers treat those who have exercised too much with more abundant oil and soft rubbing and warm baths of sweet waters that are precisely well-tempered

title: Herophilean 'three-time semeiosis'
summary: The Herophileans, like the Empiricists, introduced a three-time semeiosis: past (idle life, retained excretions), present (fullness, ulcerous sensation, heaviness) and future (benefit after evacuation).
quote: he even wrote a part of the so-called three-time semeiosis, which the followers of Herophilus introduced in the same way as the Empiricists
note: Erasistratus omitted the future part, says Galen.

title: Young Galen questions his Empiricist teacher
summary: As a youth Galen asked his Empiricist teacher whether all signs of the plethoric syndrome must concur before phlebotomy; the teacher said all must.
quote: what I myself, when I was a youth, asked my Empiricist teacher when he first taught me these things
note: Galen's Empiricist teacher is unnamed here (perhaps Aeschrion of Pergamum or another; outside knowledge, uncertain).

title: Teacher bled a man thrown from a carriage, dragged by reins
summary: Galen reminded the teacher he had bled a healthy, well-exercised man who fell from a carriage, was entangled in the reins and dragged, having only bruises; also an ophthalmia, a headache and a pleuritic.
quote: the other having fallen from a carriage and then become entangled in the reins and dragged for a considerable distance, so that certain parts were bruised
note: The teacher was left 'in the greatest perplexity'.

title: Planned discourse on phlebotomy
summary: Galen defers the full set of indications for bleeding to his discourse on phlebotomy, which no one has yet written precisely.
quote: I, since I have at present no leisure for idle talk, have decided not now, but in the discourse on phlebotomy
note: Probably De curandi ratione per venae sectionem (outside knowledge).

title: Those who make arteries and nerves 'pipes' for pneuma
summary: Galen rejects the view that faculties do not pervade solid bodies and that arteries and nerves are pipes or conduits for pneuma, refuted in PHP and Natural Faculties.
quote: who set up the arteries and the nerves as pipes or conduits for pneuma.
note: Target is Erasistratean physiology (outside knowledge).

title: Euexia, eusarkia, polysarkia; euaimia vs polyaimia
summary: Good nourishment of solids is euexia, increase of flesh eusarkia or polysarkia; good-bloodedness is natural in quality and quantity, much-bloodedness excess in quantity; in athletes faculty and blood rise together.
quote: in the case of blood there is on the one hand what is, as it were, a kind of good-bloodedness (euaimia), and on the other much-bloodedness (polyaimia).

title: Nicarchus and Praxagoras: arteries without blood
summary: Galen denies that the arterial pulse clearly shows venous plethora when thick humours block transfer, against Nicarchus and Praxagoras, who give arteries no share of blood.
quote: however much Nicarchus and Praxagoras may think so, even though they do not grant [574] the arteries any share of blood.
note: Nicarchus is obscure, perhaps a follower of Praxagoras of Cos (outside knowledge).

title: Skin colour reveals the predominant humour in plethora
summary: Blood plethora is deep red, yellow bile pale-yellow, phlegm whiter and black bile darker; bile in excess by itself, as in icterus, is cacochymia, not plethora.
quote: For the plethos of blood is deep red, that of yellow bile somewhat pale-yellow; and the colour turns toward whiter than the natural when phlegm predominates

title: Crude humour: bean-soup sediment in gluttons' urine
summary: The crude humour, thicker than phlegm, settles in urine like bean-soup sediment, especially in gluttons who avoid exercise, eat much and bathe after meals; it brings white pallor.
quote: such as settles in the urines, especially in those of people who, from gluttony, have a copious sediment resembling bean-soup
note: Only leucophlegmatic dropsy phlegm can abound through the whole body.

title: Sweet, sour and salty phlegm and their effects
summary: Sweet phlegm makes people somnolent, sour phlegm hungry, salty phlegm thirsty; the crude humour removes appetite; moist, cool sensory principle brings coma, dry hot brings sleeplessness.
quote: people become somnolent when the sweet kind is in excess, hungry when the sour kind is in excess, just as they become thirsty when the salty kind prevails
note: Greek: ὑπνώδεις ... ἐπὶ τοῦ γλυκέος, πεινώδεις ... ἐπὶ τοῦ ὀξέος, διψώδεις ... τὸ ἁλυκόν; draft matches.

title: Melancholic humour vs true black bile
summary: Black bile with acid quality makes people hungry; while it is only like a sediment of blood and not yet acid, Galen prefers to call it 'melancholic humour' rather than black bile.
quote: it is perhaps better (so far as it is called a melancholic humour) not yet to call such a humour black bile either, but, as I am accustomed, melancholic

title: What makes blood hotter, moister, colder, drier
summary: Idleness and moist regimen make blood moister; anger, exercise, sun exposure, rubbing, heating drugs or food, and stronger older wines make it hotter; recent chill colder; dry foods drier.
quote: from anger and exercises, from exposures to scorching heat and from rubbings, from a heating drug, from nourishment of that kind, and from wines less diluted and older, hotter

title: Do not diagnose plethora right after anger, bath or wine
summary: Before judging plethora from vein size and redness, wait until the effects of anger, bathing, exercise, wine or other heating have settled; then weigh heaviness, tension, pulses, sleep and appetite.
quote: it is not fitting to bring to diagnosis a man who is angry, or has bathed, or is bathing, or has exercised, or has just taken wine

title: Ranking of plethora signs; season, region, skin density
summary: Scientific signs (tension, heaviness, vein swelling, colour, pulse) outrank causes (suppressed excretions, idleness, rich food, baths after meals); winter, spring, cold regions and dense skin favour plethora.
quote: for in winter and spring, and in cold and temperate regions, people accumulate plethora more, but in hot and dry seasons and regions less
